axit = egerit,; AGIER = agi,; agentūm = agentium,) [cf. ἄγω; Sanscr. aǵ, aghāmi = to go, to drive; agmas = way, train = ὄγμος; agis = race, contest = ἀγών; perh. also Germ. jagen, to drive, to hunt], to put in motion, to move (syn.: agitare, pellere, urgere).
Lit.
Of cattle and other animals, to lead, drive.
Absol.: agas asellum, Seip. ap. : jumenta agebat,: capellas ago,: Pars quia non veniant pecudes, sed agantur, ab actu etc.,: caballum,.—
With acc. of place, prep., sup., or inf.: agere bovem Romam,: equum in hostem,: Germani in amnem aguntur,: acto ad vallum equo,: pecora per calles,: per devia rura capellas,: pecus pastum, Müll.: capellas potum age,: pecus egit altos Visere montes,.—
Of men, to drive, lead, conduct, impel.
Absol.: agmen agens equitum,.—
With prep., abl., or inf.: vinctum ante se Thyum agebat,: agitur praeceps exercitus Lydorum in populos,: (adulteram) maritus per omnem vicum verbere agit,; : captivos prae se agentes,; : acti ante suum quisque praedonem catenati,: captivos sub curribus agere,: agimur auguriis quaerere exilia,; and simple for comp.: multis milibus armatorum actis ex ea regione = coactis,.— In prose: agi, to be led, to march, to go: quo multitudo omnis consternata agebatur,: si citius agi vellet agmen, that the army would move, or march on quicker, : raptim agmine acto,; so ; .—Trop.: egit sol hiemem sub terras,: poëmata dulcia sunto Et quocumque volent animum auditoris agunto,lead the mind,. —Hence, poet.: se agere, to betake one's self, i. e. to go, to come (in Plaut. very freq.; also in Ter., Verg., etc.): quo agis te?where are you going?: unde agis te?; so ; ; ; ; : quo hinc te agis?where are you going,: Ecce gubernator sese Palinurus agebat,was moving along,: Aeneas se matutinus agebat,: is enim se primus agebat,for he strode on in front,.—Also without se: Et tu, unde agis?: Quo agis?: Huc age, (unless age is here to be taken with veni at the end of the line).—
To drive or carry off (animals or men), to steal, rob, plunder (usually abigere): Et redigunt actos in sua rura boves,.—So esp. freq. of men or animals taken as booty in war, while ferre is used of portable things; hence, ferre et agere (as in Gr. ἄγειν καὶ φέρειν, Hom. Il. 5, 484; and reversed, φέρειν καὶ ἄγειν, in Hdt. and Xen.; cf.: rapiunt feruntque,: rapere et auferre,), in gen., to rob, to plunder: res sociorum ferri agique vidit, : ut ferri agique res suas viderunt,; so ; so also: rapere agereque: ut ex alieno agro raperent agerentque,; but portari atque agi means to bear and carry, to bring together, in (as φέρειν καὶ ἄγειν in ,): ne pulcram praedam agat,: urbes, agros vastare, praedas agere,; : pecoris et mancipiorum praedas,; so eccl. Lat.: agere praedas de aliquo,; ; cf. Gron. Obs. 3, 22, 633.—
To chase, pursue, press animals or men, to drive about or onwards in flight (for the usual agitare).
Of animals: apros,: cervum,; cf. : citos canes,: feros tauros,.—
Of men: ceteros ruerem, agerem, (= prosequerer, premerem, Don.): ita perterritos egerunt, ut, etc.,: Demoleos cursu palantis Troas agebat,; cf. : aliquem in exsilium,; so ; ; ; 22, 1, 16 al.: aliquem in fugam,.—
Of inanimate or abstract objects, to move, impel, push forwards, advance, carry to or toward any point: quid si pater cuniculos agat ad aerarium?lead, make,: egisse huc Alpheum vias,made its way,: vix leni et tranquillo mari moles agi possunt,carry, build out,: cloacam maximam sub terram agendam,to be carried under ground,; so often in the histt., esp. Cæs. and Livy, as t. t., of moving forwards the battering engines: celeriter vineis ad oppidum actis,pushed forwards, up, Herz.; so ; 7, 17; ; : accelerant acta pariter testudine Volsci,: fugere colles campique videntur, quos agimus praeter navem, i. e. praeter quos agimus navem,: in litus passim naves egerunt,drove the ships ashore,: ratem in amnem,: naves in advorsum amnem,.— Poet.: agere navem, to steer or direct a ship, ; so, agere currum,to drive a chariot,; —
To stir up, to throw out, excite, cause, bring forth (mostly poet.): scintillasque agere ac late differre favillam,to throw out sparks and scatter ashes far around,: spumas ore,; so : piceum Flumen agit,: qui vocem cubantes sensim excitant, eandemque cum egerunt, etc.,when they have brought it forth,. —Hence, animam agere, to expel the breath of life, give up the ghost, expire: agens animam spumat,: anhelans vaga vadit, animam agens,: nam et agere animam et efflare dicimus,: Hortensius, cum has litteras scripsi, animam agebat,; so Cael. ap. : eodem tempore et gestum et animam ageres,: Est tanti habere animam ut agam?; and with a play upon words: semper agis causas et res agis, Attale, semper. Est, non est, quod agas, Attale, semper agis. Si res et causae desunt, agis, Attale, mulas; Attale, ne quod agas desit, agas animam,.—
Of plants, to put forth or out, to shoot, extend: (salices) gemmas agunt,: florem agere coeperit ficus,: frondem agere,: se ad auras palmes agit,: (platanum) radices trium et triginta cubitorum egisse,: per glebas sensim radicibus actis,; so : robora suas radices in profundum agunt,.—Metaph.: vera gloria radices agit,: pluma in cutem radices egerat imas,.
Trop.
Spec., to guide, govern: Tros Tyriusque mihi nullo discrimine agetur,; cf. Forbig. ad h. 1., who considers it the only instance of this use, and compares a similar use of ἄγω; v. L. and S. s. v. II. 2.—
In gen., to move, impel, excite, urge to a thing, to prompt or induce to: si quis ad illa deus te agat,: una plăga ceteros ad certamen egit,; ; : quae te, germane, furentem Mens agit in facinus? : totis mentibus acta,: in furorem agere,: si Agricola in ipsam gloriam praeceps agebatur,: provinciam avaritia in bellum egerat,.—
To drive, stir up, excite, agitate, rouse vehemently (cf. agito, II.): me amor fugat, agit,: agunt eum praecipitem poenae civium Romanorum,: perpetua naturalis bonitas, quae nullis casibus neque agitur neque minuitur, Brem.: opportunitas, quae etiam mediocres viros spe praedae transvorsos agit,i. e. leads astray,; ; so .—To pursue with hostile intent, to persecute, disturb, vex, to attack, assail (for the usu. agitare; mostly poet.): reginam Alecto stimulis agit undique Bacchi,: non res et agentia (i. e. agitantia, vexantia) verba Lycamben,: acerba fata Romanos agunt,: diris agam vos,: quam deus ultor agebat,: futurae mortis agor stimulis,; cf. Matth. ad § 21.—
To drive at something, to pursue a course of action, i. e. to make something an object of action; either in the most general sense, like the Engl. do and the Gr. πράττειν, for every kind of mental or physical employment; or, in a more restricted sense, to exhibit in external action, to act or perform, to deliver or pronounce, etc., so that after the act is completed nothing remains permanent, e. g. a speech, dance, play, etc. (while facere, to make, ποιεῖν, denotes the production of an object which continues to exist after the act is completed; and gerere, the performance of the duties of an office or calling).—On these significations, v. , and 6, 7, 64, and 6, 8, 72.—For the more restricted signif. v. ; cf. Manut. ad ; Hab. Syn. 426.
In the most gen. signif., to do, act, labor, in opp. to rest or idleness.
With the gen. objects, aliquid, nihil, plus, etc.: numquam se plus agere quam nihil cum ageret, (cf. with this, : numquam se minus otiosum esse quam cum otiosus esset): mihi, qui nihil agit, esse omnino non videtur. : post satietatem nihil (est) agendum,.—Hence,
Without object: aliud agendi tempus, aliud quiescendi,; : agendi tempora,: industria in agendo, celeritas in conficiendo,.—
In colloquial lang., to do, to fare, get on: quid agis? what are you doing? M. Tulli, quid agis? : Quid agis?What's your business?; also, How goes it with you? How are you?τι πράττεις, ; ; : vereor, quid agat,how he is,: ut sciatis, quid agam,: prospere agit anima tua,fares well,: quid agitur?how goes it with you? how do you do? how are you?; ; : Quid intus agitur?is going on,; —
With nihil or non multum, to do, i. e. to effect, accomplish, achieve nothing, or not much (orig. belonging to colloquial lang., but in the class. per. even in oratorical and poet. style): nihil agit; collum obstringe homini,: nihil agis,you effect nothing, it is of no use,: nihil agis, dolor! quamvis sis molestus, numquam te esse confitebor malum, Kühn.; Matius ap. : cupis, inquit, abire; sed nihil agis; usque tenebo,: [nihil agis,] nihil assequeris, B. and K.: ubi blanditiis agitur nihil,: egerit non multum, has not done much, Curt. ap. ; cf. Ruhnk. ad .—
In certain circumstances, to proceed, do, act, manage (mostly belonging to familiar style): Thr. Quid nunc agimus? Gn. Quin redimus, What shall we do now? : hei mihi! quid faciam? quid agam?what shall I do? how shall I act?: quid agam, habeo, (= quid respondeam habeo, Don.) al.: sed ita quidam agebat,was so acting,: a Burro minaciter actum, Burrus

proceeded to threats

, .—
To pursue, do, perform, transact (the most usual signif. of this word; in all periods; syn.: facere, efficere, transigere, gerere, tractare, curare): cui quod agat institutumst nullo negotio id agit, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 254 Vahl.): ut quae egi, ago, axim, verruncent bene, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 114 Rib.): At nihil est, nisi, dum calet, hoc agitur,: Ut id agam, quod missus huc sum,: homines quae agunt vigilantes, agitantque, ea si cui in somno accidunt, minus mirum est, Att. ap. : observabo quam rem agat,what he is going to do,: Id quidem ago,That is what I am doing,: res vera agitur,: Jam tempus agires,: utilis rebus agendis,: grassator ferro agit rem,does the business with a dagger,; (cf.: gladiis geritur res,): nihil ego nunc de istac re ago,do nothing about that matter,: postquam id actumst,after this is accomplished,; so, sed quid actumst?: nihil aliud agebam nisi eum defenderem,: ne quid temere ac fortuitu, inconsiderate negligenterque agamus,: agamus quod instat,: renuntiaverunt ei omnia, quae egerant,; : suum negotium agere,to mind one's business, attend to one's own affairs,; ; so, ut vestrum negotium agatis,: neque satis Bruto constabat, quid agerent,: postquam res in Africā gestas, quoque modo actae forent, fama divolgavit,: sed tu delibera, utrum colloqui malis an per litteras agere quae cogitas,—With the spec. idea of completing, finishing: jucundi acti labores, a proverb in .—
To pursue in one's mind, to drive at, to revolve, to be occupied with, think upon, have in view, aim at (cf. agito, II. E., volvo and voluto): nescio quid mens mea majus agit,: hoc variis mens ipsa modis agit,: agere fratri proditionem,: de intrandā Britanniā,.—
With a verbal subst., as a favorite circumlocution for the action indicated by the subst. (cf. in Gr. ἄγω with verbal subst.): rimas agere (sometimes ducere),to open in cracks, fissures, to crack,; ; : vos qui regalis corporis custodias agitis, keep watch over, guard, Naev. ap. ; so : vigilias agere,; ; : excubias alicui,: excubias,: pervigilium,: stationem agere,to keep guard,; : triumphum agere,to triumph,; ; : libera arbitria agere,to make free decisions, to decide arbitrarily,; ; : paenitentiam agere,to exercise repentance, to repent,; ; ; ; ; ; ; : silentia agere,to maintain silence,: pacem agere,: crimen agere,to bring accusation, to accuse,: laborem agere,: cursus agere,: delectum agere,to make choice, to choose,; : experimenta agere,; : mensuram,: curam agere,to care for,; , prooem. 18: curam ejus egit,: oblivia agere,to forget,: nugas agere,to trifle,; , and often: officinas agere,to keep shop,.—So esp.: agere gratias (poet. grates; never in sing. gratiam), to give thanks, to thank; Gr. χάριν ἔχειν (habere gratiam is to be or feel grateful; Gr. χάριν εἰδέναι; and referre gratiam, to return a favor, requite; Gr. χάριν ἀποδιδόναι; cf. Bremi ad ): diis gratias pro meritis agere,: Haud male agit gratias,: Magnas vero agere gratias Thaïs mihi?: Dis magnas merito gratias habeo atque ago,: Lentulo nostro egi per litteras tuo nomine gratias diligenter, : immortales ago tibi gratias agamque dum vivam; nam relaturum me adfirmare non possum,: maximas tibi omnes gratias agimus, C. Caesar; majores etiam habemus,: Trebatio magnas ago gratias, quod, etc.,: renuntiate gratias regi me agere; referre gratiam aliam nunc non posse quam ut suadeam, ne, etc.,: grates tibi ago, summe Sol, vobisque, reliqui Caelites, * : gaudet et invito grates agit inde parenti,; so ; 484; 10, 291; 681; 14, 596; ; ; and in connection with this, laudes agere: Jovis fratri laudes ago et grates gratiasque habeo,: Dianae laudes gratesque agam,; so, diis immortalibus laudesque et grates egit,: agi sibi gratias passus est,; so ; ; ; but oftener grates or gratis in Tac.: Tiberius egit gratīs benevolentiae patrum, A. 6, 2: agit grates,; ; ; ; ; 3, 24; 4, 15 al.—
Of time, to pass, spend (very freq. and class.): Romulus in caelo cum dīs agit aevom, Enn. ap. ; so Pac. , and : tempus,; : domi aetatem, Enn. ap. : aetatem in litteris,: senectutem,; cf. : dies festos,; : otia secura,; ; : ruri agere vitam,, and : vitam in terris,: tranquillam vitam agere,: Hunc (diem) agerem si,: ver magnus agebat Orbis,: aestiva agere,to pass, be in, summer quarters,; ; .—Pass.: menses jam tibi esse actos vides,: mensis agitur hic septimus,, and : melior pars acta (est) diei,; ; : acta est per lacrimas nox, Ruhnk.: tunc principium anni agebatur,: actis quindecim annis in regno,: Nona aetas agitur,—With annus and an ordinal, to be of a certain age, to be so old: quartum annum ago et octogesimum,am eighty-four years old,: Annum agens sextum decimum patrem amisit,.—Metaph.: sescentesimum et quadragesimum annum urbs nostra agebat, was in its 640th year, .— Hence also absol. (rare), to pass or spend time, to live, to be, to be somewhere: civitas laeta agere,was joyful,: tum Marius apud primos agebat,: in Africa, quā procul a mari incultius agebatur,: apud illos homines, qui tum agebant,: Thracia discors agebat,: Juxta Hermunduros Naristi agunt,: ultra jugum plurimae gentes agunt,: Gallos trans Padum agentes,: quibus (annis) exul Rhodi agit,: agere inter homines desinere,: Vitellius non in ore volgi agere,was not in the sight of the people,: ante aciem agere,; and: in armis agere, = versari.—
In the lang. of offerings, t. t., to despatch the victim, to kill, slay. In performing this rite, the sacrificer asked the priest, agone, shall I do it? and the latter answered, age or hoc age, do it: qui calido strictos tincturus sanguine cultros semper, Agone? rogat, nec nisi jussus agit,. 321 (cf. agonia and agonalia): a tergo Chaeream cervicem (Caligulae) gladio caesim graviter percussisse, praemissā voce,hoc age,; . —This call of the priest in act of solemn sacrifice, Hoc age, warned the assembled multitude to be quiet and give attention; hence hoc or id and sometimes haec or istuc agere was used for, to give attention to, to attend to, to mind, heed; and followed by ut or ne, to pursue a thing, have it in view, aim at, design, etc.; cf. Ruhnk. ad , and : hoc agite, prol. init.: Hoc age,; : Hoc agite, of poetry,: hoc agamus,: haec agamus,: agere hoc possumus,; ; , 48: hoccine agis an non? hoc agam,, ; : nunc istuc age,; : Hoc egit civis Romanus ante te nemo,: id et agunt et moliuntur,: (oculi, aures, etc.) quasi fenestrae sunt animi, quibus tamen sentire nihil queat mens, nisi id agat et adsit,: qui id egerunt, ut gentem . . . collocarent, aimed at this, that, etc., : qui cum maxime fallunt, id agunt, ut viri boni esse videantur,keep it in view, that,: idne agebas, ut tibi cum sceleratis, an ut cum bonis civibus conveniret?: Hoc agit, ut doleas,: Hoc age, ne mutata retrorsum te ferat aura,: Quid tuus ille destrictus gladius agebat?have in view, mean,: Quid aliud egimus nisi ut, quod hic potest, nos possemus?: Sin autem id actum est, ut homines postremi pecuniis alienis locupletarentur,: certiorem eum fecit, id agi, ut pons dissolveretur,: ego id semper egi, ne bellis interessem,.—Also, the opp.: alias res or aliud agere, not to attend to, heed, or observe, to pursue secondary or subordinate objects: Ch. Alias res agis. Pa. Istuc ago equidem, ; : usque eo animadverti eum jocari atque alias res agere,: atqui vides, quam alias res agamus,; : aliud agens ac nihil ejusmodi cogitans,.—
In relation to public affairs, to conduct, manage, carry on, administer: agere bellum, to carry on or wage war (embracing the whole theory and practice of war, while bellum gerere designates the bodily and mental effort, and the bearing of the necessary burdens; and bellum facere, the actual outbreak of hostile feelings, v. Herz. ad ): qui longe aliā ratione ac reliqui Galli bellum agere instituerunt,: Antiochus si tam in agendo bello parere voluisset consiliis ejus (Hannibalis) quam in suscipiendo instituerat, etc.,; : aliena bella mercedibus agere,: Bellaque non puero tractat agenda puer, (also in , Gron. Observ. 2, 3, 227, for the usu. obit, with one MS., reads agit; so Merkel).—Poet.: Martem for bellum,: agere proelium, to give battle (very rare): levibus proeliis cum Gallis actis,.—Of offices, employments, etc., to conduct, exercise, administer, hold: forum agere,to hold court,; and: conventus agere,to hold the assizes,; ; ; used of the governors of provinces: judicium agere,: vivorum coetus agere,to make assemblies of, to assemble,: censum agere,; ; : recensum agere,: potestatem agere,: honorem agere,: regnum,: rem publicam,: consulatum,: praefecturam,: centurionatum,: senatum,: fiscum agere,to have charge of the treasury,: publicum agere,to collect the taxes,: inquisitionem agere,: curam alicujus rei agere,to have the management of, to manage,; : rei publicae curationem agens,: dilectum agere, to make a levy, to levy (postAug. for dilectum habere, Cic., Cæs., Sall.), ; ; and 10; ; . —
Of civil and political transactions in the senate, the forum, before tribunals of justice, etc., to manage or transact, to do, to discuss, plead, speak, deliberate; constr. aliquid or de aliqua re: velim recordere, quae ego de te in senatu egerim, quae in contionibus dixerim,; : de condicionibus pacis,: de summā re publica,: cum de Catilinae conjuratione ageretur in curiā,: de poenā alicujus,: de agro plebis,.—Hence the phrase: agere cum populo, of magistrates, to address the people in a public assembly, for the purpose of obtaining their approval or rejection of a thing (while

agere ad populum signifies to propose, to bring before the people): cum populo agere est rogare quid populum, quod suffragiis suis aut jubeat aut vetet,: agere cum populo de re publicā,; : neu quis de his postea ad senatum referat neve cum populo agat,.—So also absol.: hic locus (rostra) ad agendum amplissimus,: Metellus cum agere coepisset, tertio quoque verbo orationis suae me appellabat,.—Transf. to common life.

Agere cum aliquo, de aliquo or re or ut, to treat, deal, negotiate, confer, talk with one about a person or thing; to endeavor to persuade or move one, that, etc.: nihil age tecum (sc. cum odore vini); ubi est ipsus (vini lepos)?I have nothing to do with you,: Quae (patria) tecum, Catilina, sic agit,thus pleads,: algae Inquisitores agerent cum remige nudo,: haec inter se dubiis de rebus agebant,thus treated together,: de quo et praesens tecum egi diligenter, et scripsi ad te accurate antea,: egi cum Claudiā et cum vestrā sorore Muciā, ut eum ab illā injuriā deterrerent,: misi ad Metellum communes amicos, qui agerent cum eo, ut de illā mente desisteret,: Callias quidam egit cum Cimone, ut eam (Elpinicen) sibi uxorem daret,.—Also absol.: Alcibiades praesente vulgo agere coepit,: si qua Caesares obtinendae Armeniae egerant,: ut Lucretius agere varie, rogando alternis suadendoque coepit,.—In Suet. once agere cum senatu, with acc. and inf., to propose or state to the Senate: Tiberius egit cum senatu non debere talia praemia tribui,.—
With the advv. bene, praeclare, male, etc., to deal well or ill with one, to treat or use well or ill: facile est bene agere cum eis, etc.,: bene egissent Athenienses cum Miltiade, si, etc.,ext.; : praeclare cum aliquo agere,: Male agis mecum,: qui cum creditoribus suis male agat,; and: tu contra me male agis,.—Freq. in pass., to be or go well or ill with one, to be well or badly off: intelleget secum actum esse pessime,: praeclare mecum actum puto,; so : exstat cujusdam non inscitus jocus bene agi potuisse cum rebus humanis, si Domitius pater talem habuisset uxorem, it would have gone well with human affairs, been well for mankind, if, etc., .—Also absol. without cum: agitur praeclare, si nosmet ipsos regere possumus, it is well done if, etc., it is a splendid thing if, etc., : vivitur cum eis, in quibus praeclare agitur si sunt simulacra virtutis,: bene agitur pro noxiā,.—
Of transactions before a court or tribunal.
Aliquid agere ex jure, ex syngraphā, ex sponso, or simply the abl. jure, lege, litibus, obsignatis tabellis, causā, to bring an action or suit, to manage a cause, to plead a case: ex jure civili et praetorio agere,: tamquam ex syngraphā agere cum populo,to litigate,: ex sponso egit,: Ph. Una injuriast Tecum. Ch. Lege agito ergo, Go to law, then, : agere lege in hereditatem,; ; : cum illo se lege agere dicebat,: summo jure agere, to assert or claim one's right to the full extent of the law, : non enim gladiis mecum, sed litibus agetur,: causā quam vi agere malle,: tabellis obsignatis agis mecum,: Jure, ut opinor, agat, jure increpet inciletque,with right would bring her charge,; so, Castrensis jurisdictio plura manu agens,settles more cases by force,: ubi manu agitur,when the case is settled by violent hands,.—
Causam or rem agere, to try or plead a case; with apud, ad, or absol.: causam apud centumviros egit,: Caesar cum ageret apud censores,; so with adversus: egi causam adversus magistratus, Esdr. 13, 11: orator agere dicitur causam,: causam isto modo agere, ; ; ; ; ; : agit causas liberales,: qui ad rem agendam adsunt, M. Cael. ap. : cum (M. Tullius) et ipsam se rem agere diceret,: Gripe, accede huc; tua res agitur,is being tried,; ; and extra-judicially: rogo ad Caesarem meam causam agas,: Una (factio) populi causam agebat, altera optimatum,; so, agere, absol., to plead' ad judicem sic agi solet, : tam solute agere, tam leniter,: tu istuc nisi fingeres, sic ageres?; and 144; 14, 32.—Transf. to common life; with de or acc., to discuss, treat, speak of: Sed estne hic ipsus, de quo agebam?of whom I was speaking,: causa non solum exponenda, sed etiam graviter copioseque agenda est,to be discussed,; : Samnitium bella, quae agimus,are treating of,.—Hence,
Agere aliquem reum, to proceed against one as accused, to accuse one, ; ; : reus agitur,; 3, 13; and with the gen. of the crime, with which one is charged: agere furti,to accuse of theft,: adulterii cum aliquo,: injuriarum,; and often in the Pandects.—
Pass. of the thing which is the subject of accusation, to be in suit or in question; it concerns or affects, is about, etc.: non nunc pecunia, sed illud agitur, quomodo, etc.,: non capitis ei res agitur, sed pecuniae,the point in dispute,: aguntur injuriae sociorum, agitur vis legum, agitur existimatio, veritasque judiciorum,: si magna res, magna hereditas agetur,: quā de re agitur, what the point of dispute or litigation is, .—Hence, trop.,
Res agitur, the case is on trial, i. e. something is at stake or at hazard, in peril, or in danger: at nos, quarum res agitur, aliter auctores sumus,: quasi istic mea res minor agatur quam tua,: agitur populi Romani gloria, agitur salus sociorum atque amicorum, aguntur certissima populi Romani vectigalia et maxima, aguntur bona multorum civium,: in quibus eorum aut caput agatur aut fama,; : non libertas solum agebatur,; : nam tua res agitur, paries cum proximus ardet, (= in periculo versatur, Lambin.): agitur pars tertia mundi,is at stake, I am in danger of losing,.—
Res acta est, the case is over (and done for): acta haec res est; perii,this matter is ended,: hence, actum est de aliquo or aliquā re, it is all over with a person or thing: actum hodie est de me,: jam de Servio actum,: actum est de collo meo,.—So also absol.: actumst; ilicet me infelicem,: si animus hominem pepulit, actumst,; ; : actumst, ilicet, peristi,: periimus; actumst,.—
Rem actam agere, to plead a case already finished, i. e. to act to no purpose: rem actam agis,; ; ; so, actum or acta agere: actum, aiunt, ne agas,; : acta agimus,.—
To represent by external action, to perform, pronounce, deliver, etc.
Of an orator, ; cf. : quae sic ab illo acta esse constabat oculis, voce, gestu, inimici ut lacrimas tenere non possent,: agere fortius et audentius volo,; .—
Of an actor, to represent, play, act: Ipse hanc acturust Juppiter comoediam,; so, fabulam,; : dum haec agitur fabula,: partīs,to have a part in a play,: Ballionem illum cum agit, agit Chaeream,: gestum agere in scaenā,: dicitur canticum egisse aliquanto magis vigente motu,—Transf. to other relations, to represent or personate one, to act the part of, to act as, behave like: has partes lenitatis semper egi, : egi illos omnes adulescentes, quos ille actitat,: amicum imperatoris,: exulem,: socium magis imperii quam ministrum,: senatorem,.—So of things poetically: utrinque prora frontem agit,serves as a bow,.—
Se agere = se gerere, to carry one's self, to behave, deport one's self: tantā mobilitate sese Numidae agunt,: quanto ferocius ante se egerint, Halm: qui se pro equitibus Romanis agerent,: non principem se, sed ministrum egit,: neglegenter se et avare agere,: prudenter se agebat,: sapienter se agebat,. —Also absol.: seditiose,: facile justeque,: superbe,: ex aequo,: anxius et intentus agebat,.—
Imper.: age, agite, Ter., Tib., Lucr., Hor., Ov., never using agite, and Catull. never age, with which compare the Gr. ἄγε, ἄγετε (also accompanied by the particles dum, eia, en, ergo, igitur, jam, modo, nuncjam, porro, quare, quin, sane, vero, verum, and by sis); as an exclamation.
In encouragement, exhortation, come! come on! (old Engl. go to!) up! on! quick! (cf. I. B. fin.). (α In the sing.: age, adsta, mane, audi, Enn. ap. Delr. Synt. 1, 99: age i tu secundum,come, follow me!: age, perge, quaeso,: age, da veniam filio,: age, age, nunc experiamur,: age sis tu ... delude,; ; ; : quanto ferocius ante se egerint, agedum eam solve cistulam,; : Agedum vicissim dic,; : agedum humanis concede,: age modo hodie sero,: age nuncjam,: En age, quid cessas,: Quare age,: Verum age,: Quin age,: en, age, Rumpe moras,: eia age,.—
In the plur.: agite, pugni,up, fists, and at 'em!: agite bibite,; : agite in modum dicite,: Quare agite ... conjungite,; : vos agite ... volvite,: agite nunc, divites, plorate,: agitedum,.—Also age in the sing., with a verb in the plur. (cf. ἄγε τάμνετε, Hom. Od. 3, 332; ἄγε δὴ τραπείομεν, ): age igitur, intro abite,: En agedum convertite,: mittite, agedum, legatos,: Ite age,: Huc age adeste,.—
In transitions in discourse, well then! well now! well! (esp. in very freq.). So in Plaut. for resuming discourse that has been interrupted: age, tu interea huic somnium narra, Curc. 2, 2, 5: nunc age, res quoniam docui non posse creari, etc., well now, since I have taught, etc., : nunc age, quod superest, cognosce et clarius audi,; so ; ; ; 730; 3, 418; 4, 109 al.: age porro, tu, qui existimari te voluisti interpretem foederum, cur, etc.,; so ; ; .—And age (as in a.) with a verb in the plur.: age vero, ceteris in rebus qualis sit temperantia considerate,; so ; ; .—
As a sign of assent, well! very well! good! right! Age, age, mansero, : age, age, jam ducat; dabo,: Age, veniam,: age, sit ita factum,: age sane,; .!*? Position.—Age, used with another verb in the imperative, regularly stands before it, but in poetry, for the sake of the metre, it,
Sometimes follows such verb; as,
In dactylic metre: Cede agedum,: Dic age,; ; : Esto age,: Fare age,: Finge age,: Redde age,: Surge age,; ; ; : Vade age,; ; so, agite: Ite agite,.—
In other metres (very rarely): appropera age,: dic age,,

32, 3; 2, 11, 22; 3, 4, 1.—So also in prose (very rarely): Mittite agedum,: procedat agedum ad pugnam,.—

It is often separated from such verb: age me huc adspice,; : Age ... instiga,; : Quare agite ... conjungite,: Huc age ... veni,: Ergo age cervici imponere nostrae,: en age segnis Rumpe moras,: age te procellae Crede,: Age jam ... condisce,; .—Hence,
ăgens, entis, P. a.
Adj.
Efficient, effective, powerful (only in the rhet. lang. of Cic.): utendum est imaginibus agentibus, acribus, insignitis,: acre orator, incensus et agens,.—Comp. and sup. not used.!*?
Agentia verba, in the grammarians, for verba activa, .—
Subst.: ăgentes, ium.
Under the emperors, a kind of secret police (also called frumentarii and curiosi), ; ; ; ; 22; 23, etc.; ; —
For agrimensores, land-surveyors, .—
actus, a, um, P. a.Lit., that has been transacted in the Senate, in the forum, before the courts of justice, etc.; hence,
actum, i, n., a public transaction in the Senate, before the people, or before a single magistrate: actum ejus, qui in re publicā cum imperio versatus sit,: acta Caesaris servanda censeo,: acta tui praeclari tribunatūs,.—
acta publĭca, or absol.: acta, ōrum, n., the register of public acts, records, journal. Julius Cæsar, in his consulship, ordered that the doings of the Senate (diurna acta) should be made public, ; cf. Ernest. Exc. 1; but Augustus again prohibited it,. Still the acts of the Senate were written down, and, under the succeeding emperors. certain senators were appointed to this office (actis vel commentariis Senatūs conficiendis), . They had also public registers of the transactions of the assemblies of the people, and of the different courts of justice; also of births and deaths, marriages, divorces, etc., which were preserved as sources of future history.—Hence, diurna urbis acta,the city journal,: acta populi,: acta publica,; ; : urbana,; which were all comprehended under the gen. name acta.
With the time added: acta eorum temporum,: illius temporis,: ejus anni,.—
Absol., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : Quis dabit historico, quantum daret acta legenti, i. e. to the actuarius, q. v., ; cf. Bähr's Röm. Lit. Gesch. 303.—
acta triumphōrum, the public record of triumphs, fuller than the Fasti triumphales, .—
acta fŏri (v. ), the records,
Of strictly historical transactions, ; .—
Of matters of private right, as wills, gifts, bonds (acta ad jus privatorum pertinentia, ), Fragm. Vat. §§ 249, 266, 268, 317.—
acta mi-litarĭa, the daily records of the movements of a legion, .

la:noun:ager.html:
ăger, gri, m.
ἀγρός; Germ. Acker, Eng. acre, Sanscr. agras = surface, floor; Grimm conjectured that it was connected with ago, ἄγω, a pecore agendo, and this was the ancient view; cf. Müll., and Don. ad ; so the Germ. Trift = pasture, from treiben, to drive
.
In an extended sense, territory, district, domain, the whole of the soil belonging to a community (syn.: terra, tellus, arvum, solum, rus, humus; opp. terra, which includes

many such possessions taken together; cf. Nieb. Röm. Gesch. 2, 694 sq.): Ager Tusculanus, ... non terra,: praedā atque agro adfecit familiares suos,: abituros agro Achivos,: ut melior fundus Hirpinus sit, sive ager Hirpinus (totum enim possidet), quam, etc.,: fundum habet in agro Thurino, id. Fragm. ap. (pro Tull. 14): Rhenus, qui agrum Helvetium a Germanis dividit, Herz.: ager Noricus,: in agro Troade,: in agro Aretino,: his civitas data agerque,: in agro urbis Jericho,.—In the Roman polity: ager Romanus, the Roman possessions in land (distinguished from ager peregrinus, foreign territory) was divided into ager publicus, public property, domains, and ager privatus, private estates; v. Smith's Dict. Antiq., and Nieb. Röm. Gesch. 2, 695 and 696; cf. with 153 sq.—

In a more restricted sense.
Improdued or productive land, a field, whether pasture, arable, nursery ground, or any thing of the kind; cf. Doed. Syn. 3, 7 sq.; 1, 71; Hab. Syn. 68, and Herz. ad : agrum hunc mercatus sum: hic me exerceo,: agrum de nostro patre colendum habebat,: ut ager quamvis fertilis, sine culturā fructuosus esse non potest,; : agrum colere,: conserere,: agrum tuum non seres,: (homo) seminavit bonum semen in agro suo,; . —* Of a piece of ground where vines or trees are planted, a nursery: ut ager mundus purusque flat, ejus arbor atque vitis fecundior,.—Of a place of habitation in the country, estate, villa: in tuosne agros confugiam, (so ἀγρός, Hom. Od. 24, 205).—
The fields, the open country, the country (as in Gr. ἀγρός or ἀγροί), like rus, in opp. to the town, urbs (in prose writers generally only in the plur.), : homines ex agris concurrunt,: non solum ex urbe, sed etiam ex agris,: annus pestilens urbi agrisque,; : in civitatem et in agros,.—And even in opp. to a village or hamlet, the open field: sanum hominem modo ruri esse oportet, modo in urbe, saepiusque in agro,.—
Poet., in opp. to mountains, plain, valley, champaign: ignotos montes agrosque salutat,.—
As a measure of length (opp. frons, breadth): mille pedes in fronte, trecentos cippus in agrum Hic dabat,in depth,.

la:adj:agrestis.html:
ā^grestis, e, adj.
id.
.
Lit., pertaining to land, fields, or the country, country, rural, rustic, wild, ἄγριος: Musa,: te in Arpinati videbimus et hospitio agresti accipiemus,: vestitus,: falx,: poma,: cum lactucis agrestibus,: ligna non sunt pomifera, sed agrestia,: herbas agrestes,.—Subst.: ā^gre-stis, is (gen. plur. agrestūm, ), a countryman, rustic, farmer, peasant, : non est haec oratio habenda aut cum imperitā multitudine aut in aliquo conventu agrestium,: collectos armat agrestes,: Fictilia antiquus primum sibi fecit agrestis Pocula,: facinus admissum a quodam agresti,: inopes agrestes,; .—
Transf., and in mal. part.
Rustic, in opp. to the refined citizen (urbanus, as ἄγριος is opp. to ἀστεῖος), boorish, clownish, rude, uncultivated, coarse, wild, savage, barbarous, of persons and things: sunt quidam vultu motuque corporis vasti atque agrestes,: O rem dignam, in quā non modo docti, verum etiam agrestes erubescant,: aborigines, genus hominum agreste,: Ego ille agrestis, saevos, tristis, parcus, truculentus, tenax Duxi uxorem,: quis nostrūm tam animo agresti ac duro fuit, ut, etc.,: dominus agrestis et furiosus,: exculto animo nihil agreste, nihil inhumanum est,; so : rustica vox et agrestis,; . —Hence, agrestiores Musae, ruder, of the language of the bar, in opp. to more refined and polished eloquence, .—
Wild, brutish: vultus,: agrestem detraxit ab ore figuram Juppiter (of Io),.—Comp., v. above.— * Sup. agrestissimus, .— * Adv. comp. neutr. agrestius, .

la:verb:agito.gloss: to act, behave, do, or make persistently or unremittingly
senses: to act, behave, do, or make persistently or unremittingly
to put something in motion, drive, impel; drive by rowing, row about; shake, throb
to drive to and fro, toss about, agitate, disturb, churn
to rouse or stir up, excite, move, urge, drive or impel someone to something, insist on
to disturb, disquiet, provoke, agitate, vex, trouble, torment
to reprove, assail, blame, decry, scoff, deride, insult, mock
to be engaged in, do, accomplish, have, hold, keep; celebrate; practise, exercise
la:verb:agito.html:
ăgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.
ago
, as if the supine were
agitu; cf.: quaero quaerito.
Lit., to put a thing in motion, to drive or impel (mostly poet., or in more elevated prose; from poetry it passed, after the Aug. per., into common prose).
Of cattle, to drive, conduct (cf. ago): calcari quadrupedem agitabo advorsum clivom,: stimulo boves agitat,: hanc in curru bijugos agitare leones,drives her span of lions,: agitantur quadrigae, Müll.: ad flumina currus,: jussit agitari currum suum,: lanigeros greges hirtasque capellas, to drive, poet. for to tend, : sacros jugales (dracones),: quadrigas bigasque et equos desultorios,.—
Of the motion of other things, to move, impel, shake: triremem in portu,: alas,: manibusque leves agitavit habenas,: hastam,: caput, to move the head (in token of assent = annuere), : arundinem vento agitatam,.—Esp., of animals, to hunt, chase, pursue: etiamsi excitaturus

non sis nec agitaturus feras, : aquila insectans alias aves atque agitans,: trepidas columbas,; : damas,: cursu timidos onagros,—

Of the motion caused by the wind, to drive to and fro, toss about, agitate, disturb: ventus enim fit, ubi est agitando percitus aër,when the air is violently agitated and driven,: mare ventorum vi agitari atque turbari,; : freta ponti Incipiunt agitata tumescere,: aristas,: Zephyris agitata Tempe,: ventis agitatur pinus,: veteres agitantur orni,: agitaret aura capillos,.—
Of the motion caused by the water: agitata numina Trojae, tossed or driven about upon the sea, ; .—
In gen., of the motion caused by other things: magnes (lapis) agitat (ferri ramenta) per aes,: agitari inter se concursu,: pulsu externo agitari, Macr Somn. Scip. 9.—Poet. of mist, to produce it by motion or agitation: dejectuque (Peneus) gravi tenues agitantia fumos Nubila conducit, and by its impetuous descent (into the valley) raises clouds producing mist, —
Trop.
To rouse up, excite, move, urge, drive, impel one to something: aliquem, sometimes in aliquid (so in Florus very freq.): in furias agitantur equae,are excited to fury,: agitare plebem,to stir up, rouse,: populum,; so : agitatus cupiditate regni,: gens sacratis legibus agitata in exitium urbis,.—
To disquiet, disturb, to drive hither and thither, to vex, trouble, torment (the fig. taken from the sea agitated by storm; cf. Gernh. and Beier upon ): dii deaeque te agitant irati,: atra bilis agitat hominem,; so ; : ut eos agitent furiae, neque usquam consistere patiantur, (cf. : scelerum furiis agitatus Orestes,): suum quemque scelus agitat amentiaque afficit,: agitare et insequi poëtas,; and 41: multis injuriis jactata atque agita ta,: est magni viri, rebus agitatis (= perturbatis, Beier) punire sontes,: agitabatur animus inopiā rei familiaris et conscientiā scelerum,: quos conscientia defectionis agitabat,: commotus metu atque libidine diversus agitabatur,was drawn in different directions,; . ne te semper inops agitet vexetque cupido, : quos agitabat timor,: timore et metu agitati,: injuriis agitatus,: seditionibus,.—
To assail with reproach, derision, insult; to reprove, blame, scoff, deride, insult, mock: agitat rem militarem, insectatur totam legationem,attacks, ridicules,; : mea saevis agitat fastidia verbis, Hor Epod. 12, 13; without verbis: agitant expertia frugis,: vesanum poëtam agitant pueri,.—
In gen., to drive or urge on a thing, to accomplish or do, to drive at, to be employed in, be engaged in, to have, hold, keep, to celebrate; v. ago, II. D. (in the historians, esp. Sallust, very freq.): Haec ego non agitem?should I not drive at?: vigilias,to keep,; so, custodiam,; so : hoc agitemus convivium vino et sermone suavi,let us celebrate,: Dionysia,; so : convivia,; festa gaudia, : meum natalem,; so festos dies,: jocos,: agraria lex a Flavio tribuno plebis vehementer agitabatur,was powerfully urged, supportcd,: quae cum praecepta parentis mei agitarem,was striving to comply with, (modestius dictum pro: studere, ut agerem, Cort.): laeti pacem agitabamus,were at peace, enjoyed the delights of peace,: dicit se missum a consule venisse quaesitum ab eo, pacem an bellum agitaturus foret,: quoniam deditionis morā induciae agitabantur,there was a truce,; .— Poet.: ceu primas agitant acies, certamina miscent,as if they formed the front rank,.—Hence of time, esp. life, to pass, spend (cf. ago, II. D 5.): vita hominum sine cupiditate agitabatur,: agitare aevum,; : festos dies,.—In Sall., Tac., Flor., et al., agitare absol., to live, dwell, abide, sojourn, be: hi propius mare Africum agitabant,; cf ; ; so ; ; : laeti Germant agitabant,: secretus agitat,: montium editis sine cultu atque eo ferocius agitabant,; .—
Of the mind: agitare aliquid or de aliquā re (in corde, in mente, animo, cum animo, secum, etc.), to drive at a thing in the mind, i. e. to turn over, revolve, to weigh, consider, meditate upon, and with the idea of action to be performed or a conclusion to be made, to deliberate upon, to devise, contrive, plot, to be occupied with, to design, intend, etc.: id ego semper mecum sic agito et comparo, Att ap. : quom eam rem in corde agito,: id agitans mecum,; so : habet nihil aliud quod agitet in mente,: est tuum sic agitare animo, ut, etc.,: quae omnes animo agitabant,: provincias secretis imaginationibus agitans, in animo bellum, Liv 21, 2; ; .—With inf., as object: ut mente agitaret bellum renovare,.—Poet.: aliquid jamdudum invadere magnum Mens agitat mihi,. —Sometimes also without mente, animo, and the like, agitare aliquid, in the same signif: quodsi ille hoc unum agitare coeperit, esse, etc.,: rem a me saepe deliberatam et multum agitatam requiris,: oratori omnia quaesita, disputata, tractata, agitata (well considered or weighed) esse debent, : fugam,.—So esp. freq. in Tac.: Britanni agitare inter se mala servitutis, Agr 15: bellum adversus patrem agitare,, ; .—With de: de bello,: agitanti de Claudio,: de tempore ac loco caedis agitabant,; 1, 12; .—With num: agitavere, num Messalinam depellerent amore Silli,; .— With -ne: agitavere placeretne, etc.,.—With an: an Artaxata pergeret, agitavit,—With quomodo, .—With ut (of purpose): ut Neronem pudor caperet, insita spe agitari,.—
To treat or speak of or concerning a thing, to confer about, deliberate upon. Romae per omnīs locos et conventus de facto consulis agitart (impers., for agitabatur), discussions were had, ; cum de foedere victor agitaret,; .—*
Sat agitare, with gen., in Plaut., = sat agere, to have enough to do, to have trouble with: nunc agitas sat tute tuarum rerum, Bacch. 4, 3, 23.

ăgĭtātor, ōris, m.

he that puts a thing in motion; used exclusively of those who drive animals (asses, horses, etc.), a driver (cf. agaso): agitator aselli, poet. for a peasant, : equorum Achillis,i. e. the charioteer,: sustineat currum ut bonu' saepe agitator equosque, Müll.—Hence,

la:noun:Agamemnon.html:
Ăgămemnon, ŏnis, m. (nom. Agamemno, Enn. ap. ; ; ), = Ἀγαμέμνων,
king of Mycenœ, son of Atreus and of Aërope, brother of Menelaüs, husband of Clytœmnestra, father of Orestes, Iphigenia, and Electra, commander-in-chief of the Grecian forces before Troy, and murdered by his wife, with the aid of Ægisthus, her paramour.—Poet., for his time: vixēre fortes ante Agamemnona Multi,- 28.—Hence,
ăgămemnŏnĭdēs, ae, patr. m., = Ἀγαμεμνονίδης, a male descendant of Agamemnon; his son Orestes: par Agamemnonidae crimen,i. e. the matricide of Orestes,.—
ăgămem-nŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = Ἀγαμεμνόνιος, of or pertaining to Agamemnon (poet.): phalanges,i. e. the Grecian troops before Troy, commanded by Agamemnon,: Mycenae,ruled by Agamemnon,: Orestes,son of Agamemnon,: puella, daughter of Agamemnon, i. e. Iphigenia, .

la:noun:agmen.html:
agmĕn, ĭnis, n.
as if contr. from agimen, from ago; cf.: tegimen, tegmen, from tego
.
Lit.
In gen., a train, i. e. a collected multitude in motion or moving forwards; of things of any kind, but esp. (so most freq. in prose) of men or animals. —Of streams of water, motion, course, current: quod per amoenam urbem lent fluit agmine flumen, Enn. ap. : inde super terras fluit agmine dulci,; cf. ; also, in imitation of Enn., Virg. and Val. Fl.: leni fluit agmine Thybris,; cf. .—Of a train or succession of clouds: denso sunt agmine nubes,.—Of rain: immensum caelo venit agmen aquarum,body, mass, —Of atoms: agmine condenso naturam corporis explent,crowded into a compact mass,.—Of oars: agmine re morum ceieri,with quick plashing of oars,.—Of a flock of birds: agmi ne magno. Corvorum. .—Of a snake winding onwards: cum medii nexus extremaeque agmina caudae Solvuntur,; cf. .—Of clouds of dust following any thing in rapid motion, as men, animals, etc.: agmina cervi Pulverulenta,.—And, as subst. concr., of birds turba Agminis aligeri, of the winged band, Verg A. 12, 249.—Of ants; frugilegas aspeximus agmine longo formi cas,; so .—Of the stars: diffugiunt stellae; quarum agmina cogit Lucifer,; so al.—Eap. of a company of persons, a multitude, troop, crowd, number, band: ut a Brundisic nsque Romam agmen perpetuum totius Italiae viderem,: magno senatorum agmine,: ingens mulierum agmen,: muliebre et miserabile agmen,: numerosum agmen reorum, Plin Ep. 3, 9, and : Eumenidum agmina, Verg A. 4, 469.—But particularly,
The train, procession, march, progress of an army: de castris, de agminibus, etc., dicere,: ne miles gregarius in castris, neve in agmine servum aut jumentum haberet,: pugnatum saepe directā acie, saepe in agminibus, saepe eruptionibus,: effuso agmine abire,: uno agmine victores cum victis in urbem irrupere,; uno agmine persequentes,—
Transf., concr., an army, and properly considered as in motion, on the march (while exercitus is a disciplined army, and acies an army in battle-array) —As soon as the signal for marching was given, the Extraordinarii and the allies of the right wing, with their baggage, first put themselves in motion, then the legions, and last the allies of the left wing, with a part of the cavalry, which either rode behind the army, ad agmen claudendum or cogendum. to close the train, i. e. to keep it to gether or on the side in such an order (composito agmine, non itineri magis apto quam proelio) that it might be easily put into the line of battle, if the enemy ven tured to attack it; cf. .—An army in close ranks was called agmen justum, , or agmen pilatum, —When there was no apprehension of the enemy, less care was taken for the protection of the army: agmine incauto, i. e. minus munito, ut inter pacatos, ducebat, sc. consul,.— The order of march was, however, different, according to circumstances and the nature of the ground,; ; and cf. Smith's Antiq.—Sometimes the army marched in the form of a square, agmen quadratum, with their baggage in the middle, so as to be in battle-array on meeting the enemy; hence agmen quadratum often means the same as acies triplex, an army formed in line of battle, only that the former indicates that they are on the march, and the latter that they are at rest.—Hence, like acies, with the epithet primum, the vanguard, ; : medium,the centre,; : extremum,; ; or, novissimum,the rear, rearguard,; so, extremi agminis,: ut inde agmine quadratc ad urbem accederet,marching in a square,: pariter atque in conspectu hostium quadrato agmine incedere,; cf. : Hannibal agmine quadrato amnem ingressus,; se ; : quadrato agmine velut in aciem irent,—Sometimes, esp. in the poets in the plur., in gen.

P.: virtus cum se extollit et ostendit suum lumen et idem aspexit agnovitque in alio,and when she has perceived the same in another, and has recognized it,: id facillime accipiunt animi, quod agnoscunt,: cum se collegit (animus) atque recreavit, tum agnoscit illa reminiscendo,: quod mihi de filiā gratularis, agnosco humanitatem tuam, (cf. on the contr. , where Cic., speaking of himself, says: Cognosce nunc humanitatem meam, learn from this, etc.): nomine audito extemplo agnovere virum,: veterem amicum,: matrem,: Figulum in patriam suam venisse atque ibi agnosci, and is there recognized (by those who had already known him), : formas quasdam nostrae pecuniae agnoscunt,: agnoscent Britanni suam causam,: nitorem et altitudinem horum temporum agnoscimus,: quam (tunicam) cum agnovisset pater,.—

To understand, recognize, know, perceive by, from, or through something: ut deum agnoscis ex operibus ejus, sic ex memoriā rerum et inventione, vim divinam mentis agnoscito,; : ex fructu arbor agnoscitur,: inde agnosci potest vis fortunae,.—Also, absol.: Augusti laudes agnoscere possis, you can recognize the praises of Augustus, * : accipio agnoscoque deos, (cf. accipio): agniti dempsere sollicitudinem,: Germanicus, quo magis agnosceretur, detraxerat tegimen,: terram non agnoscebant,.—In gen., to become acquainted with, to know; to perceive, apprehend, understand, discern, remark, see: quin puppim flectis, Ulixe, Auribus ut nostros possis agnoscere cantus, (as transl. of Hom. Od. 12, 185, Νῆα κατάστησον, ἵνα νωϊτέρην ὄπʼ ἀκούσῃς): haec dicta sunt subtilius ab Epicuro quam ut quivis ea possit agnoscere,understand,; ; : alienis pedibus ambulamus, alienis oculis agnoscimus,.
